title: Shortest routes that touch a line
sections: Let A and B lie strictly on the same side of a straight line, and let B′ be the reflection of B in that line. For every contact M on the line, AM + MB = AM + MB′ ≥ AB′. Equality holds exactly when M is the crossing of the segment AB′ with the line. Thus the unrestricted shortest two-leg route has one unique contact.

For a permitted closed segment of the line, the same construction proves optimality only if its crossing is permitted. If that contact is excluded, the lower bound AB′ is not attained there; it does not identify the new constrained optimum. Equal lengths of some trial routes do not imply that either is shortest.

Reflection preserves the distance from every point on its line. This also explains why two reflected destinations give equal route lengths at every common contact. The theorem concerns Euclidean length, one straight boundary and one contact; it does not assert a rule for curves or multiple bounces.
K–1: Build legal two-leg routes, compare string lengths, and notice equal-length or shorter alternatives. The adult demonstrates one legal bend and one path that illegally runs along the boundary.
Grades 2–3: Use a fold or tracing to preserve a leg, find a candidate, and check the permitted contact. Explore inverse constructions and equalities.
Grades 4–5: Use an arbitrary rival M to justify a universal lower bound, its attainment and uniqueness; distinguish contact constraints from the unconstrained theorem.

A string experiment suggests a best route; a conjecture says which route should always win; reflection plus the straight-line inequality explains why every allowed rival is no better. Read the longer proof on printed page 3 and the problem keys afterward.
